title: Marda and the Sparkle-Snatchers
markdown:
The sun, a golden coin, laid long shadows across the Silver Passes of Cloudneedle Ridge, where ancient peaks practised touching cloud. Marda the young ogre tended a patch of bushy herbs with hands like dinner plates, good for weeding and for holding too many sandwiches. She loved her home, the smell of wild thyme, the rumbling laugh of ogres at stew-time. Still her heart leaned past the familiar slopes toward lands where clouds might taste of spun sugar and mountains wore snow like crowns. The world beyond the doorstep kept secrets. She intended, someday, to ask them politely.

Weeding moonwort, she overheard two stout goats by an old oak, moss in their beards, voices like downhill pebbles.

“They say,” bleated Cressida, nudging Bartholomew with a horn like polished agate, “in the Whispering Woods there are sparkle-snatchers.”

“Steal the gleam from pebbles and dew from leaves? Nonsense,” said Bartholomew, eyes saucer-wide.

Marda’s oak-leaf ears twitched. Silly. Important. Adventure weather.

Mother, amber-kind: “Far, little one. Paths are clearer here.” Father, stone-crushing hands, gentle: “Shadows play. Ground tricks. Who knows what lurks.”

Mind aflutter like a butterfly that had heard a rumour and believed it. Sparkle-snatchers were too curious to leave on a goat’s tongue. She would investigate. Trusted companions first.

Bramble the badger: big grumbles, unwavering loyalty, fur like a rough warm rug, a nose that could find a ripe berry from a mile and a complaint from two. “Hmph. Sparkle-snatchers. Nonsense. If you’re chasing silliness, someone should keep you from getting lost.”

Pip the marmot: quick, jumpy, often startled by himself, whiskers full of questions. “Are they very fast? Sharp teeth? Will there be puddles? I do dislike puddles.” Tiny paws tapped a worried rhythm.

“We’ll be careful. We’ll stick together. A grand look, not a grand fight.” Rucksack: extra-large cheese sandwiches, a flask of berry juice, a heart trying on brave purpose and finding it fitted well enough.

The woods had no grand gate. Ancient ivy hung a curtain, dark and wet with dew, a secret door if you were willing. They stepped under. Air cooler, damp earth, flowers that had been old since last year. Sunlight made bright coins on the ground. Tall trees stood like wise faces, branches fingered the sky. Moss and leaf made their steps quiet, which Pip considered both kind and suspicious. The woods felt huge and, somehow, like a room sharing secrets. “Whiskers tingling,” Pip whispered. “Earthy. Wet socks. Also sweet, honeyed flowers.” “That’s the forest breathing,” Marda said, though her own tummy fluttered like a small bird that had heard the word adventure.

Sticky webs, moonlight-fine, steel-strong. Pip ensnared, tail jam-sandwich. Bramble, helping, stuck ears and all. “Blast. Inconvenient.” Marda’s large fingers, surprisingly kind to threads, freed them. Pip emerged a decorated nest. “Alarming.” “Ticklish,” Bramble sniffed.

Giggle-mushrooms: hee-hee, and if you laughed too hard you floated. Pip yelped into a giggle and drifted. Marda caught him. Bramble’s ho-hos lifted his shoulders; she anchored him too. “No floating. Sparkle business.”

After more careful stepping—around a root that looked like a question, past a puddle Pip detoured with ceremony—they found the sparkle-snatching. Not a fearsome monster. Tiny iridescent sprites, Mistlings no bigger than dragonflies, scooping dew with desperate hands, flicking wings to catch shimmer off stones. Frantic beat. One, jewel-toned, clutched a small woven basket. The basket had a gaping hole. As they collected light, it tumbled through like clumsy stars.

Losing, not stealing. Trying to make up the leak before a festival. Marda’s heart did the softening it did for wilted thyme.

Marda stepped out, rumble gentle. They shrank, glow dim. “Don’t hurt us.”

“Marda. Bramble. Pip. We heard snatchers. You’re losing shimmer.”

Wail, silver-bell. “Moonpetal Festival tonight. Dim and sad without enough. The basket—” Reeds loose, captured light trickling like fallen stars.

“Not meanness. Mending.” She knelt, shadow a comfort. Bramble to sniff fallen gleam. Pip to gather, quick and careful. Her own fingers wove thick green vines through the gaps, herb-garden skill turned small. Mistlings pointed best stems with tiny light. Basket whole, stronger, almost handsome.

Bramble found pools of moonlight-dew. Pip scooped. Mistlings added their catch. The basket overflowed soft radiance, brighter than any theft.

Night came in the useful way. The Moonpetal Festival was not dim. Woods glowed warm and friendly; Mistlings danced; laughter like tiny bells that had been tuned. Marda, Bramble, and Pip watched from a decent rock, the sort of distance that lets a party be itself. Satisfaction, deep, no need to join the reel.

Home along the Silver Passes, moon painting the ridge, sandwiches gone, juice flask honest. Stew later, and one telling at table: not a hunt for villains, a hole that needed hands. They did not ask the forest to remember. Bramble grunted that the webs had been ticklish. Pip checked for puddles on the doorstep. Marda put her dinner-plate hands in the herb water and felt, for once, that adventure had fitted them.
characters: Marda (Marda the young ogre), Bramble (mountain companions)
